description_full: PagerDuty, Inc. engages in the operation of a digital operations management platform in the United States and internationally. The company collects data and digital signals from virtually any software-enabled system or device and leverages artificial intelligence and powerful machine learning to correlate, process, predict, and remediate incident. Its platform includes PagerDuty Incident Management that provides a real-time view status of a digital service; AIOps that applies machine learning to correlate and automate the identification of incidents from billions of events; automation that offers centralized design time and run time environment for orchestrating automated workflows; customer service operations, which is offered to orchestrate, automate, and scale responses to customer issues; and artificial intelligence that offers generative AI capabilities for the PagerDuty operations cloud platform. The company serves various industries, including software and technology, telecommunications, retail, travel and hospitality, media and entertainment, and financial services. PagerDuty, Inc. was founded in 2009 and is headquartered in San Francisco, California.

financial_summary: PagerDuty, Inc. is a small-cap technology business with a $1.2B market cap on $493M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +5.8pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at -128% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 83% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $112M in free cash flow — roughly 23 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.66×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.7× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 10.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and stock-based comp at 20% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insiders hold 9.1% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 1% operating margin trails the Technology median (7%) by 6pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.05x its revenue share).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 13% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 69% and a beta of 1.35, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.15 vs 5y 1.66), so read it loosely.
About $22.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash and 48% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $5.94 (margin of safety -164%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 61%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $4.92 to $7.49 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Technology peers: cheaper on P/E 7.8 vs 26.7 and P/FCF 11.0 vs 25.4, richer on EV/EBITDA 26.6 vs 16.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 9.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $12.86 on average, 18% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 20.8% annual cash-flow growth, 19pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 128% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.8%, so growth at these returns destroys value.
It runs a 83% gross margin and converts 23% of revenue into free cash flow, or 3% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9, but cash conversion of only 0.66x.
ROE of 68% is amplified by 3.9x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
Operating margin is running 25pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 25.8% of revenue on R&D and 19.9% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $49.2M (4% of market cap).
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.32 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
The Beneish M-score (-1.84) sits just under the manipulation line, so earnings quality bears watching.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 9.9% over 3 years and 18.2% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
Free cash flow has compounded 79.2% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.02 and a backlog worth 91% of annual revenue.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (0.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 21, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 9.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 98%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $7.1M sold).
It returns 10.9% a year to shareholders (10.9% in buybacks).
Short interest is elevated at 11.9% of the float, 4.5 days to cover.
people: With about 1,155 employees, each generates about $426K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and productivity has risen 19.8% a year.
That works out to $97K of free cash flow per employee.
Compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
